rv.q: Neither prosaic nor clinical, it defies all expectations for a story in which the main character receives a fatal diagnosis, telling the tale in the most lively, surreal and surprising ways imaginable.

I almost feel guilty having enjoyed it as much as I did. But playwright Noah Diaz, making his New York debut, has so artfully stitched together the real world and some far-off galaxy of his imagination, and fused the funny with the sad, that 'You Will Get Sick' emerges as a highly original pick-me-up.
If you give this Roundabout Theatre Company world premiere by Noah Diaz a chance, you will find a delightfully strange new play full of magic and wonder.
Under Sam Pinkleton’s tight direction, this loopy lockdown-era play is simultaneously sobering and side-splitting.
You Will Get Sick is ultimately an engaging effort, sustaining its 90-minute length due to its strong emotional core and the supreme Linda Lavin.
Lavin is center stage for most of the play, and so it works very well indeed.
It walks the finest of lines and sometimes it trips.

You Will Get Sick prompts more confusion than clarity, but a healthy helping of dry humor (particularly from Lavin) and a commitment to being daring and experimental for its own sake make it entertaining.
But his preference for an idiosyncratic style of storytelling renders “You Will Get Sick” largely indecipherable, thought the production is at times entertaining.
Over an interminable eighty-five minutes, playwright Noah Diaz’s You Will Get Sick meanders between absurdity and inanity, continually challenging the audience to distinguish one from the other.

Sam Pinkleton’s often clever direction, supported by the stylishly abstract scenery of dots, and the well-balanced chiaroscuro of Cho See’s lighting, goes a long way to capturing the play’s eccentricities.

cn.t: Diaz's absurdist meditation on mortality and caregiving divides critics: some praise its inventive staging and Lavin's performance, finding it charming and thought-provoking, while others dismiss it as indecipherable and meandering despite striking moments.
